title: Batch processing vs Stream processing — Spark batch for historical analysis, Flink/Kafka Streams for real-time.

s1_definition.profdef: Batch processing operates on a large, bounded dataset collected over a period, running a job to completion and producing results in one pass, optimized for throughput over latency; Apache Spark is a common engine. Stream processing operates on an unbounded, continuous flow of events, computing results incrementally with low latency as data arrives; Apache Flink and Kafka Streams are common engines. The choice depends on whether you need high-throughput analysis of historical data or low-latency reaction to events as they happen.
s1_definition.analogy: At the end of each day, National Bank of India gathers every transaction and runs one big job to compute interest and reports — that is batch processing, done on a fixed pile of data overnight. But the fraud team needs to catch a suspicious transaction within seconds of it happening, so they watch the live stream of transactions and react immediately — that is stream processing. Batch is the overnight accountant working through yesterday's ledger; streaming is the security guard watching the cameras in real time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Batch processes a bounded dataset in one high-throughput pass (Spark); streaming processes an unbounded event flow with low latency as it arrives (Flink/Kafka Streams).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Batch processing operates on a large, bounded dataset collected over a period, running a job to completion and producing results in one pass, optimized for throughput over latency; Apache Spark is a common engine. Stream processing operates on an unbounded, continuous flow of events, computing results incrementally with low latency as data arrives; Apache Flink and Kafka Streams are common engines. The choice depends on whether you need high-throughput analysis of historical data or low-latency reaction to events as they happen.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the end of each day, National Bank of India gathers every transaction and runs one big job to compute interest and reports — that is batch processing, done on a fixed pile of data overnight. But the fraud team needs to catch a suspicious transaction within seconds of it happening, so they watch the live stream of transactions and react immediately — that is stream processing. Batch is the overnight accountant working through yesterday's ledger; streaming is the security guard watching the cameras in real time.

**One line to remember:** Batch processes a bounded dataset in one high-throughput pass (Spark); streaming processes an unbounded event flow with low latency as it arrives (Flink/Kafka Streams).

sections.s2_technical:
Batch processing takes a bounded dataset, often a day's or month's worth of data at rest, and runs a job over all of it. It optimizes for throughput: it can crunch enormous volumes efficiently because it sees the whole dataset and can schedule work across a cluster. The latency is high because results are available only after the job completes. Spark is the dominant engine, reading from storage, transforming in stages, and writing results.

```java
// Batch (Spark-style): process a full day's transactions at once
Dataset<Row> txns = spark.read().parquet("/data/transactions/2026-10-31");
Dataset<Row> interest = txns.groupBy("accountId")
    .agg(sum("amount").multiply(lit(0.0001)).as("dailyInterest"));
interest.write().parquet("/data/interest/2026-10-31");   // results after full pass
```

Stream processing consumes an unbounded flow of events and computes results incrementally as each event or small window arrives, optimizing for low latency. It maintains state over time, uses windows to group events by time, and must handle event-time versus processing-time, watermarks for late data, and checkpointing for fault tolerance. Flink and Kafka Streams are common engines, continuously reading from a topic and emitting updated results.

```java
// Stream (Kafka Streams-style): react to each transaction within seconds
builder.stream("transactions")
    .filter((k, txn) -> isSuspicious(txn))           // react immediately
    .to("fraud.alerts");                              // emit as events arrive
```

The decision is driven by latency need and data boundedness. Use batch when you need to analyze large historical datasets, when results can wait minutes or hours, and when correctness over a complete dataset matters, such as end-of-day interest calculation, regulatory reports, and reconciliation. Use streaming when you need to react within seconds, such as fraud detection, real-time dashboards, and live alerts. A senior nuance is that the two often coexist in a unified architecture: streaming handles the real-time path and batch handles periodic recomputation and backfills, and modern engines increasingly treat batch as a special case of streaming over a bounded source, so the same logic can sometimes run both ways, with the key design point being that a bounded job is streaming's special case, not a wholly different paradigm.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must compute daily interest for every account and produce regulatory reports over the complete set of the day's transactions. The real problem is high-throughput analysis of a bounded dataset where completeness matters. This is exactly what batch processing provides.

Problem 2 — the fraud team must flag a suspicious transaction within seconds of it occurring, not the next morning. The real problem is low-latency reaction to a continuous event flow. This is exactly what stream processing provides.

Problem 3 — the bank wants both: real-time fraud alerts and a nightly reconciliation that recomputes totals over the full day. The real problem is combining both paradigms coherently.

We build a runnable core modelling both: a `BatchProcessor` that aggregates a full list of transactions in one pass for interest and totals, and a `StreamProcessor` that reacts to each transaction as it arrives, flagging suspicious ones immediately. The demo runs the stream over a live sequence flagging fraud in real time, then runs the batch over the whole day for interest and a reconciliation total.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a day's list of five transactions, including one large suspicious amount, processed first as a stream and then as a batch.

Step 1: The stream processor handles each transaction one at a time as it arrives. For each, it updates a running per-account total, which is the kind of state streaming maintains. Normal transactions are logged as processed.

Step 2: When the large six hundred thousand transaction arrives, the stream immediately compares it to the suspicious threshold and raises a real-time fraud alert, right then, not the next morning. This immediacy is the whole point of streaming.

Step 3: The batch processor then takes the entire day's list at once and groups by account, summing each account's amounts and multiplying by the interest rate to compute daily interest per account. Because it sees the complete dataset, the result is correct over the whole day.

Step 4: The batch processor also reduces all amounts into a single reconciliation total, which is a completeness-oriented computation that makes sense only over the full bounded dataset. The data that changed is the stream's running state and real-time alert versus the batch's complete-dataset aggregates.

```
2026-11-01 03:10:00 [INFO] STREAM processing (real-time fraud):
2026-11-01 03:10:00 [INFO] stream processed SAV2001 Rs.50000
2026-11-01 03:10:00 [WARNING] FRAUD ALERT (real-time): SAV2001 Rs.600000
2026-11-01 03:10:00 [INFO] BATCH processing (end-of-day):
2026-11-01 03:10:00 [INFO] daily interest: {SAV2001=67.0000, CUR3001=1.5000}
2026-11-01 03:10:00 [INFO] reconciliation total = 685000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Day's transactions
    │
    ├─ STREAM path (low latency)         ├─ BATCH path (throughput)
    │  onEvent(t) for EACH txn           │  computeDailyInterest(ALL txns)
    │  update running state              │  groupBy account → sum × rate
    │  amount > threshold?               │  reconcileTotal(ALL txns)
    │   └─ FRAUD ALERT now               │   → one pass, complete result
    ▼                                    ▼
  react within seconds               results after full job

  Lambda-style: stream = real-time view, batch = authoritative recompute
```

  react within seconds?       → STREAM (Flink/Kafka Streams)

sections.s6_takeaway:
Batch and stream processing are two paradigms for computing over data, and I choose by latency need and whether the data is bounded. Batch processing operates on a large, bounded dataset collected over a period, running a job to completion in one high-throughput pass. It is optimized for throughput, not latency, so results are available only after the job finishes, which is perfectly fine for work that can wait. Apache Spark is the dominant engine, and in banking I use batch for end-of-day interest calculation, regulatory reports, and reconciliation, where correctness over the complete dataset is what matters.

Stream processing operates on an unbounded, continuous flow of events, computing results incrementally with low latency as each event arrives. It maintains state over time, groups events into time windows, and must handle event-time versus processing-time, watermarks for late data, and checkpointing for fault tolerance. Apache Flink and Kafka Streams are the common engines, and in banking I use streaming for fraud detection, real-time dashboards, and live alerts, where reacting within seconds is the entire value. In the demo, the stream flagged a suspiciously large transaction the instant it arrived, rather than the next morning.

The two are not competitors so much as complements, and modern architectures run both. The streaming path handles the real-time reactions, like fraud alerts, while the batch path handles periodic, authoritative recomputation over the full day, like interest and reconciliation. At National Bank of India, that means a fraud alert fires in seconds on the stream, while overnight a Spark batch job recomputes the complete, correct totals and reports.

The senior insight I bring is that batch is increasingly understood as a special case of streaming over a bounded source, so the same aggregation logic can often run both ways, and engines are converging toward this unified model. The key design decision is therefore not a religious choice of one paradigm but matching each workload to the right path: low-latency reactions go to the stream, and high-throughput, completeness-oriented analysis goes to batch, with a unified architecture letting them reinforce each other rather than duplicating effort.
